how-github-actions-minutes-are-billed.ht.text:
How GitHub Actions minutes are billed

The arithmetic a GitHub Actions cost estimate is built from. No signup, nothing to install.

Most people meet Actions billing for the first time when something stops working — a wall of red checks, or a number on an invoice nobody expected. The rules are not complicated, but three of them are counter-intuitive enough that a workflow can cost five or ten times what its author assumed.

1. Private repositories draw on a monthly allowance

Each plan includes a number of minutes per month. Public repositories run free on standard runners and have no allowance to exhaust.

PlanIncluded minutes / month
Free2,000
Pro3,000
Team3,000
Enterprise Cloud50,000

Past the allowance you are billed per minute, if a spending limit allows it. If it does not, jobs simply stop being assigned runners — which is what the wall of red usually is.

2. The operating system multiplies what you spend

This is the first surprise. A minute is not a minute: what a standard runner draws from your allowance depends on the image.

RunnerAllowance minutes per wall minute
Linux (ubuntu-*)1×
Windows (windows-*)2×
macOS (macos-*)10×

A ten-minute test suite on macOS spends a hundred allowance minutes. On the Free plan, twenty such runs consume the entire month. The common shape that triggers this is not a deliberate choice at all — it is runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }} over an OS matrix, where the macOS leg quietly outspends the other two put together.

3. Every job is rounded up, separately

The second surprise. Rounding is per job, not per workflow run. Thirty matrix jobs of twenty seconds each are billed as thirty minutes, not ten — the rounding costs three times the work.

This makes a wide matrix of very short jobs one of the worst value shapes available. Combining several axis values into a single job that loops over them removes the rounding entirely.

4. Larger runners are billed differently

Larger GitHub-hosted runners (ubuntu-latest-8-cores and similar) are charged per minute from the first minute and do not draw on the included allowance. They do not make you run out of minutes; they appear on the bill instead. Self-hosted runners are free to Actions — you are paying for the hardware somewhere else.

5. A job with no timeout can run for six hours

The third surprise, and the one that does the most damage in a single incident. If a job does not set timeout-minutes, GitHub lets it run for 360 minutes before killing it. One hung job — a test waiting on a port that never opens, a command sitting at an interactive prompt — bills 360 minutes on Linux, and 3,600 on macOS. That single wedged job exceeds the entire monthly allowance of every plan below Enterprise.

Setting timeout-minutes a little above a job's normal runtime costs nothing and caps the worst case.

6. Two events can build the same commit twice

A workflow that triggers on both push and pull_request, with no branches: filter on push, runs twice for every commit pushed to a branch with an open pull request. Both runs are genuine, so nothing in the billing page marks either as waste. Restricting push to your default branch keeps the main-branch run and drops the duplicate.

Relatedly, without a concurrency group set to cancel-in-progress: true, pushing three times in a row leaves the first two runs going to completion and billing in full, even though nobody will look at their results.

7. Scheduled workflows bill whether or not anything changed

A cron of */20 * * * * is about 2,190 runs a month. At three minutes a run that is 6,570 allowance minutes — more than twice the Team allowance — accruing on a repository nobody is touching. Scheduled spend is the easiest kind to forget, because no pull request is ever associated with it.

Questions

Why does a macOS minute cost ten times a Linux minute?

GitHub applies a multiplier per runner image when drawing down your included allowance: Linux 1x, Windows 2x, macOS 10x. The wall-clock time is the same; what differs is how many allowance minutes it consumes. A ten-minute test suite on macOS spends a hundred allowance minutes, so twenty such runs consume the entire Free plan month.

Does a job that takes twenty seconds cost twenty seconds?

No. Each job is rounded up to the next whole minute, and the rounding is per job rather than per workflow run. Thirty matrix jobs of twenty seconds each bill thirty minutes, not ten, so the rounding costs three times the work. Combining several matrix axis values into one job that loops over them removes it.

How long can a job run if I do not set timeout-minutes?

360 minutes. GitHub kills it only at that point, so one hung job — a test waiting on a port that never opens, a command sitting at an interactive prompt — bills 360 minutes on Linux and 3,600 on macOS. That single wedged job exceeds the entire monthly allowance of every plan below Enterprise.

Do larger runners use up my included minutes?

No. Larger GitHub-hosted runners are charged per minute from the first minute and do not draw on the included allowance, so they appear on the bill rather than making you run out of minutes. Self-hosted runners are free to Actions — you are paying for that hardware elsewhere.

Why would the same commit be built twice?

A workflow that triggers on both push and pull_request, with no branches filter on push, runs twice for every commit pushed to a branch with an open pull request. Both runs are genuine, so nothing in the billing page marks either as waste. Restricting push to your default branch keeps the main-branch run and drops the duplicate.

Paste your workflow YAML and get projected monthly minutes and cost, attributed per workflow and per job, with these patterns flagged where they appear.

GITHUB ACTIONS MINUTES ESTIMATOR · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

What will this workflow cost you a month?

GitHub's billing page shows you minutes you have already spent, added up across the whole account. It will not tell you which workflow spent them, and it cannot tell you what the workflow in your open pull request is about to cost. Paste your workflow YAML below and this does the arithmetic forward — per workflow, per job, with the expensive patterns named.

Nothing is uploaded. Parsing and costing happen in this browser and are never sent anywhere.

1. Paste your workflow files

One file, or several separated by a line of ---. Everything in .github/workflows/ is the useful answer; a single file tells you about that file.

2. Set your assumptions

These drive every number. Scheduled runs are counted exactly from each cron expression; everything else depends on how busy your repository is, which only you know.

Projected monthly cost

Where it goes

WorkflowJobRunner Runs/moJobsAllowance min

Findings

Assumptions behind these numbers

    Run it in your own CI

    The same estimator is a zero-dependency Node CLI. Wired into a workflow with a budget, it fails the build when a change pushes projected usage past a share of your allowance — which is the only moment anyone finds out before the minutes are gone.

    node cli.mjs .github/workflows
node cli.mjs --plan free --minutes-per-job 8 .github/workflows
node cli.mjs --json .github/workflows          # machine-readable
node cli.mjs --max-allowance-percent 80 .github/workflows   # exit 1 when over

    Download cli.mjs, estimate.mjs and workflow-yaml.mjs and keep them next to each other. Node 18+, nothing to install, no network access required or used.

    How the billing actually works

    The multipliers and the per-job rounding are where most of the surprise lives. How GitHub Actions minutes are billed explains the arithmetic this tool uses and why a wide matrix of short jobs can bill several times its wall-clock time.

    Already out of minutes and staring at a wall of red checks? actions-runner-starvation-check tells you whether a red check is a real failure or a job GitHub never assigned a runner to — the thing that happens after the allowance is spent.

    Comparing CI vendors rather than estimating one workflow? Price GitHub Actions, CircleCI, GitLab, Bitbucket and Buildkite side by side at your build-minute volume.

    Already reading your GitHub billing page and wondering what this adds? See this estimator vs. your billing page.

    Think eyeballing the workflow file and doing the multiplication yourself gets you close enough? See this estimator vs. doing the math yourself for the three rules that go wrong by hand.

    Questions

    Why can't I just read my GitHub billing page?

    Billing shows minutes you have already spent, aggregated across the account. It does not attribute them to a workflow or a job, and it cannot tell you what a workflow you are about to merge will cost. This reads the workflow files and does the arithmetic forward, so the answer arrives before the allowance does.

    How are GitHub Actions minutes billed?

    On private repositories, each plan includes a monthly allowance of minutes. Standard runners consume that allowance at a multiplier by operating system: Linux 1x, Windows 2x, macOS 10x. Each job's duration is rounded up to the next whole minute independently, so a wide matrix of very short jobs bills far more than its wall-clock time. Public repositories run free on standard runners.

    What is the most common avoidable cost?

    A workflow that triggers on both push and pull_request with no branches filter on push. A commit pushed to a branch with an open pull request fires both events, so the whole workflow runs twice on the same commit. Both runs are real, so nothing in the billing page marks one of them as waste.

    Is my workflow file uploaded anywhere?

    No. The page parses and costs everything in your own browser and sends nothing anywhere. There is no account and no analytics vendor. The CLI reads local files and makes no network call at all.

    Are the dollar figures exact?

    No, and they are not meant to be. They are an estimate built from your workflow files plus assumptions you set — how long a job takes, how often you push. Every assumption is shown on screen and is editable, and the published list rates being quoted are dated. Check the result against your own billing page before making a decision on it.

vs-billing-page.html.text:
← GitHub Actions Minutes Estimator

This tool vs. reading your GitHub billing page

Your GitHub billing page is the only place that shows what you actually paid. It is authoritative, and nothing here replaces it as the number to reconcile against. What it does not do is attribute that number to a workflow, a job, or a matrix leg, and it cannot tell you anything about a workflow you have not merged yet -- it only reports minutes already spent, added up across the whole account.

This tool reads the workflow YAML you paste and runs the same billing arithmetic GitHub applies -- the OS multiplier, per-job rounding, the free plan's included minutes -- forward, before you merge, and attributes the projected cost per workflow and per job. It answers a different question than billing does: not "what did I spend" but "what is this about to cost."

QuestionWhere to answer it
What did my account actually get charged last month? Your GitHub billing page -- it is the source of truth for money that already moved.
What will this workflow I'm about to merge cost, before it runs once? This estimator -- billing has no answer for a workflow that has not run yet.
Which job or matrix leg is actually spending my allowance? This estimator -- billing reports one aggregated number for the whole account, not a breakdown per workflow or job.
I want this checked automatically before a change merges, failing the build if it pushes usage over budget. This estimator's CLI -- node cli.mjs --max-allowance-percent 80 .github/workflows exits non-zero, wired into CI itself.

In practice the two are used together: this tool before a change merges, to catch an expensive pattern while it is still a diff, and the billing page afterward, to confirm the account actually spent what was projected.

Try it

Paste the workflow file you are about to change and see the projected monthly cost, with the expensive patterns named, before it reaches your billing page at all.

Estimate a workflow's cost

Free, runs entirely in your browser, nothing is uploaded. Already out of minutes and staring at red checks instead? actions-runner-starvation-check tells you whether a red check is a real failure or a job GitHub never assigned a runner to.

Questions

Should I stop checking my GitHub billing page if I use this tool?

No. The billing page is the only place that shows what you were actually charged, and it is the source of truth to reconcile against. This tool exists for the question the billing page cannot answer -- what a workflow you have not merged yet, or one you are changing right now, will cost -- so the two are complementary rather than substitutes.

Why can I not just watch the billing page after each merge?

You can, but by then the minutes are already spent, and the billing page still will not tell you which workflow or which job spent them -- it reports a single aggregated number for the account. Attributing that total back to a specific matrix leg or a specific cron schedule is arithmetic you would have to do by hand, from memory of what changed and when, on every workflow you suspect.

Do I need to know the billing rules myself to use this tool?

No, and that is most of what it replaces. The multipliers, the per-job rounding, and the free-minutes-only-on-public-repos rule are exactly the arithmetic this tool applies to your pasted YAML, so you do not have to re-derive them from GitHub's documentation each time you want an answer for a specific workflow. How GitHub Actions minutes are billed explains that arithmetic in full if you want to check the tool's working.

Is my workflow file uploaded anywhere to get this estimate?

No. Parsing and costing happen entirely in your own browser and nothing is sent anywhere -- there is no server this portfolio operates that ever sees the YAML you paste. The CLI version reads local files and makes no network call at all, which is the same trust boundary as running grep on your own repository.

vs-doing-the-math-yourself.html.text:
← GitHub Actions Minutes Estimator

This tool vs. doing the math yourself

Doing the math yourself usually means multiplying a job's wall-clock minutes by how often it runs, and stopping there. That gets close on a single small Linux job. It goes wrong in three specific, easy-to-miss ways once a workflow uses a different runner class, a matrix, or a larger runner -- each below with the real arithmetic and a number worked through this tool's own code, not hand-computed.

This tool reads the workflow YAML and applies the same three rules automatically, per job and per matrix leg, so a number it prints has already accounted for all three.

Mistake 1: forgetting the OS multiplier

A minute on a macOS runner does not draw one minute from your included allowance -- it draws 10 (Windows draws 2; Linux draws 1). Hand math that just adds up wall-clock minutes treats every runner the same.

Worked example: a macOS job that runs 15 wall-clock minutes a month. Naive math: 15 minutes against the allowance. What actually happens, run through estimate():

  • Wall-clock minutes: 15
  • Included-allowance minutes actually drawn: 150 -- ten times the naive figure, because RUNNER_CLASSES.macos.multiplier is 10.

On a Free plan's 2,000-minute allowance, that one job alone is 7.5% of the month's included minutes -- from something hand math would have logged as a rounding error.

Mistake 2: rounding a matrix once instead of per job

GitHub rounds each job's duration up to the next whole minute, and it does that per job, not per workflow run. Hand math that multiplies total wall-clock time by a rate rounds once, at the end -- which is the wrong place to round when a matrix is involved.

Worked example: a 12-shard test matrix, each shard finishing in 30 seconds. Naive math: 12 × 0.5 = 6 minutes billed. Run through the same estimate() call:

  • Wall-clock minutes: 6
  • Billed minutes: 12 -- exactly double, because each of the 12 legs rounds its 0.5 minutes up to a full minute on its own before anything is summed.

The gap grows with the matrix, not with the job: a 40-shard matrix at 15 seconds each is 10 wall-clock minutes and 40 billed minutes, a 4x gap from the same rounding rule.

Mistake 3: larger runners drawn from the wrong pool

A larger GitHub-hosted runner (an -8-cores label, for instance) is billed per minute from the first minute, priced per core, and does not draw from your included allowance at all. Hand math tends to either fold it into the same allowance a standard runner uses, or skip it because "it's free minutes like the rest" -- both read the rule backwards.

Worked example: an 8-core Linux runner, 6 wall-clock minutes per run, 120 runs a month (roughly one push an hour during a working day). Run through estimate():

  • Total wall-clock minutes: 720
  • Included-allowance minutes drawn: 0 -- none of this comes out of the free allowance
  • Direct cost: $23.04 a month, billed separately, at $0.004 per core-minute across 8 cores

A workflow using this runner can look free in a spreadsheet that only tracks "minutes against the allowance" -- the allowance column reads zero while the account is actually being charged.

What hand math usually assumesWhat actually happens
A minute is a minute, whatever the runner macOS draws 10x, Windows 2x, against the included allowance
Round the total once, at the end Every job rounds up to a whole minute on its own, before the matrix is summed
A larger runner's minutes count the same as a standard runner's Larger runners bill per core-minute from minute one, outside the included allowance entirely

Try it

Paste a workflow file and get the same three rules applied automatically, per job and per matrix leg, instead of re-deriving them by hand each time.

Estimate a workflow's cost

Free, runs entirely in your browser, nothing is uploaded. Want the arithmetic itself rather than the tool's output? See how GitHub Actions minutes are billed. Already reading your billing page too? See this estimator vs. your billing page.

Questions

Is eyeballing a workflow file really that unreliable?

For a single small job on a Linux runner, hand math gets close enough. It stops working the moment any of three things are true: a job runs on macOS or Windows, a job is part of a matrix, or a job uses a larger runner -- each of those changes the arithmetic in a way that is easy to apply backwards from memory, and this tool exists because getting any one of them wrong understates the real bill by a wide margin.

What is the single easiest mistake to make by hand?

Treating a larger runner's minutes as if they draw from the same included allowance as a standard runner. They do not -- a larger runner is billed per minute from the first minute, outside the free allowance entirely, which is the opposite of how a standard macOS or Windows job behaves. Getting this backwards is the single easiest way to project a cost of zero for a job that is actually the most expensive one in the file.

Why does a matrix of short jobs cost more than the wall-clock time suggests?

GitHub rounds each job's duration up to the next whole minute, and it does that per job, not per workflow run. A matrix of twelve 30-second jobs is 6 minutes of wall-clock work, but it is twelve separate roundings to a full minute each -- 12 billed minutes, double the wall-clock figure. Multiplying total wall-clock time by a single per-minute rate misses this because it rounds once instead of twelve times.

Do I need to know the billing rules myself to use this tool?

No, and that is the point of it. The OS multipliers, the per-job rounding, and the larger-runner allowance rule are exactly the arithmetic this tool applies to your pasted YAML, so a number it prints has already accounted for the three mistakes on this page without you having to re-derive them by hand.
